of scholars not to have been written by Paul, but to have been written by someone only pretending to be Paul and probably decades after his death. Hey
everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and religion. And these two passages are 1 Corinthians 14 34 and 35
and 1 Timothy 2 11-15. And they both say more or less the same thing, that women not only are not allowed to have
authority, they're not even allowed to talk in church. And one of the first indications that this is probably not Paul writing is that at least the
passage in 1 Corinthians 14 directly contradicts Paul's discussion in 1 Corinthians chap 11 regarding women
praying and prophesying in church. And there Paul just says they need to have a head covering on. So scholars have long pointed to this disagreement as an
indication this might be an interpolation in chapter 14. And the manuscript evidence also is suggestive
of that given the two passages that talk about women remaining silent and not speaking are found in other parts of this chapter in a couple of manuscripts.
And if you would like a recent discussion of the evidence for seeing verses 34 and 35 as an interpolation or
a textual addition to 1 Corinthians chapter 14, you can check out this recent open access paper by Richard
Fellows. Now, when it comes to 1 Timothy chapter 2, the majority of scholars agree that all of the pastoral epistles,
so 1 and 2 Timothy as well as the epistle of Titus, were probably written by someone pretending to be Paul toward the end of the 1st century CE or more
likely in my opinion, the beginning of the 2 century CE. And scholars began to argue for this perspective at the beginning of the 19th century. But it
had become the majority view by the beginning of the 20th century. And if you would like the most thorough discussion, I think Raymond Collins
book, Letters that Paul Did Not Write from 1988 gives a really good overview.
And Collins also published in 2002 a commentary on first and second Timothy as well as Titus where he reviews some of this discussion as well. You can also
look in Bartman's book Forged as well as in this commentary on first and second Timothy and Titus by Annette Huisena
from the wisdom commentary which is a feminist commentary series. And I frequently get asked when I point this out what the argument is. And I'm not
going to actually make the argument in this video, but I'm happy to highlight what scholars have pointed to as the
data that suggest the pastoral epistles are not from Paul. one is that they all seem to agree on the majority of the things that they're talking about. So,
whoever the author of first and second Timothy and Titus was probably the same author and then they also seem to agree
with each other over and against the perspectives of the genuine Pauline epistles. And this is linguistic. This is theological. This is ecclesiastical.
This even has to do with Paul's own personal history. A lot of folks have pointed out that the journeys that are described in the pastoral epistles don't
fit within the narrative that we can reconstruct from the genuine Pauline epistles as well as from the acts of the apostles. We have to make some
assumptions and jin up some scenarios in order to make what is described in the pastoral epistles fit into the narrative
that we can reconstruct from those other two sets of texts. Now, we also have the linguistic differences. There is an
awful lot of terminology in the pastoral epistles that is not used anywhere else in the genuine Pauline epistles or even anywhere else in the New Testament. And
when we look at when that language is used, about a third of the unique terms that are used in the pastoral epistles aren't used in first century CE
literature and are very common in 2 century CE literature. There's also the development of the church. It's a much
more developed ecclesiastical framework that is referred to throughout the pastoral epistles. Whereas within the
genuine Pauline epistles written in the middle of the first century CE, it's more of a charismatic movement than an
institutionalized church framework. And so scholars have pointed out that is suggestive of someone writing later on.
And there's also a lot of theological differences. Paul is very big on righteousness. Paul is very big on this kind of mystical being in Christ. Paul
is very big on the soma, the body. And these things are either never addressed at all in the pastor oral epistles or if
they are addressed are addressed in very different ways where being in Christ just means being a Christian. It is not
the mystical union that is described in the genuine Pauline epistles. And then there's also some external evidence. The
pastoral epistles are omitted from some of our earliest manuscripts that contain the Pauline epistles as a group or the
entire New Testament. And we also have a couple of people such as Marcion who is widely condemned as a heretic in the
second century CE who was a huge Paul Stan. His entire cannon was Paul and then a specific version of Luke. But he did not include the pastoral epistles.
And Tatan the author of the Deotesseron also suggested that some early Christians did not accept the authority
of the pastoral epistles. And so we have internal and external evidence for the pseudapographic origins of the pastoral
epistles probably in the first or second decade of the 2 century CE. And while none of these pieces of evidence on
their own definitively proves Paul could not have been the author, they make it less likely that Paul is the author. And
when we combine them all, it becomes entirely implausible that Paul could have written the pastoral epistles. And obviously, folks who believe in the
inherency and the inspiration and the historicity of the New Testament are going to find reasons to disagree with
this. And that's fine. You can go publish your arguments. You can change the consensus view. But you'll see that in a lot of scholarship that tries to
deny this argument, they're beginning from a rather dogmatic position. For instance, this pastoral epistles volume in the international theological
commentary series by Gerald Bray actually says the epistles are innocent until proved guilty, which places an
unreasonable and a dogmatic burden of proof on the majority of scholars who agree the data do not support the
Pauline authorship of the pastoral epistles.
1 Timothy chapter 2 is the only other place where we find Paul denying ecclesiastical authority to women. And we even see elsewhere in the genuine
Pauline epistles references by Paul to women who hold ecclesiastical authority.
And I think most prominently in my opinion Romans 16:7 which refers to Junia as an apostle. So again, the only
